svg.title: Inter-AS L3VPN options A, B and C: which router holds the VRF, which holds the VPN routes, and what each costs
svg.desc: Three rows, one per option, each showing the ASBR to ASBR relationship and four facts: VRFs on the ASBR, whether VPNv4 is carried across the boundary, the session count and the operational cost. Option A keeps back-to-back VRFs on the two ASBRs, so no VPN route crosses the AS boundary; it is the easiest to explain and the hardest to scale, since each VPN needs a subinterface and a session on the boundary. Option B carries VPNv4 between the ASBRs, so no per-VRF subinterface is needed, but the ASBR must hold VPN routes and labels for every VPN and is the scaling bottleneck. Option C keeps VPN routes only on the PEs and reflectors, with the ASBR forwarding labelled packets and exchanging labelled IPv4 routes or using a multi-hop session; it scales best and is the hardest to troubleshoot. A bottom band gives the decision rule by number of VRFs and by the trust boundary between the two providers.
svg.text: Inter-AS: three options, and the trade is always the same one
A pushes complexity to the boundary, B pushes it onto the ASBR, C pushes it into the design
Option A · back-to-back VRF on the ASBRs
ASBR-1
ASBR-2
one subinterface + one session per VPN
+ nothing crosses the boundary that a normal router cannot understand
+ easiest to explain to a partner, easiest to debug
− session and subinterface count grows with VPNs, not with sites
Option B · MP-eBGP VPNv4 between the ASBRs
ASBR-1
ASBR-2
one MP-BGP session carries every VPN
+ no per-VPN subinterface on the boundary
+ any number of VRFs over a single session
− the ASBR holds every VPN route and label: it becomes the scaling limit
Option C · multi-hop MP-eBGP between PEs, ASBR forwards labels only
ASBR-1
ASBR-2
labelled packets only, no VPN routes here
+ VPN routes stay on PEs and reflectors: scales furthest
+ ASBR carries labelled IPv4 under a route-reflector design
− two label layers, next-hop-unchanged and RR policy must all be right; hardest to debug
Decision rule: a handful of VRFs and an untrusted partner boundary → A. One provider, many VRFs, one operational team → B.
Two large providers or a carrier core with hundreds of VPNs → C, and budget the engineering time for it.
